chunks: "It depends on the fault and how bad the consequence is, so I think of it as a menu from gentle to drastic.
The gentlest response is just to flag it: set a status bit or interrupt so firmware knows and can log it or throttle the load.
Next is limiting: a current-limited regulator or foldback holds the current at a safe value so the system keeps running at reduced power.
If limiting isn't enough, I shut down: turn off the converter or open a series switch. Here the restart policy matters.
Latch-off stays off until someone resets it, which is safest but needs intervention.
Auto-retry tries again after a delay, and hiccup mode does short attempts with long pauses, so a persistent short only sees a few percent duty and the average heating is small.
For overvoltage, I can clamp with a TVS or crowbar the rail and blow a fuse, or disconnect the load with an OVP switch.
I'd also make the response match the speed of the hazard: nanoseconds for a spike, microseconds for a short, milliseconds for an overload.
And for an embedded system I'd use the warning to enter a safe state: stop the motors, save to non-volatile memory using hold-up capacitance, and reset cleanly."
